title: Prompting Strategies
tagline: Why prompts work — three levers, sixty-four hand-written answers, zero network
hub_blurb: Change one prompt lever at a time—context, a success specification, or expert vocabulary—and see exactly what each contributes.
card_blurb: A question sits beside three toggleable levers, and the answer changes in exactly one dimension per lever. Sixty-four hand-written answers, each labelled as hand-written on the panel that shows it, a deck that decides your answer’s shape whenever you don’t, and a meter counting the expert vocabulary you got for free.
description: **Prompting Strategies** (the roleplay is called *The Stranger*) — why prompts work, for a classroom. A student's question sits beside three toggleable blocks — context, success spec, expert keywords — and all 64 answers across four scenarios are hand-written and baked into the file, ~25,700 words. Every answer renders under a permanent **Scripted** label reading “hand-written example answer — no model runs here”, because the panel that shows an answer is the surface that makes the claim. A content gate in `tools/validate.py` (a manual step, *not* the build) fails if any two of the 64 share more than 5% of their sentences; current worst is 0.00%. The levers-off answers are deliberately competent and aimed at nobody, so the room cannot dismiss the demo as rigged. Three stages are the three levers, each opening with a question, a prerequisite refresh and a captured prediction whose result is echoed beside it. Two stage mechanics: a target deck inside lever 2 that deals itself a card whenever nobody has said what a finished answer looks like — labelled a teaching device, since a real model does not draw from three cards — and a jargon meter whose count is the author's tag list (Scripted) while its “words you never typed” check is computed live. Class scoring plots usefulness against levers pulled, carrying a Reasoned note that the answers were written to improve, so the curve shows the room agreeing with the author rather than a measurement of AI. Each stage closes with a check-yourself item with feedback on every option, and stage 3 adds a documented first-party case: a brief that asked for 100% accuracy, got claims that were all true, and produced an aggregate picture that was wrong. The printable presenter sheet, with eight cut-out target cards, is also the presenter notes inside the app: one file, injected at build time, with a check that fails on drift.
